title: Thalamus Atlas
subtitle: Map the relay, association and regulatory nuclei linking cortex, subcortex and arousal systems
altText: Clinically labelled chalkboard-style anatomical illustration of the thalamus atlas, showing major subdivisions, connections and nearby landmarks.
learningObjectives: Locate the thalamus relative to the third ventricle, internal capsule and basal ganglia.
Differentiate major relay, association and intralaminar nuclear groups.
Connect thalamic vascular territories and pathway disruption to plausible clinical signs.

sections.explainSimply: The thalamus is a paired hub deep in the brain. Most sensory information, and many motor and attention signals, pass through specialised thalamic nuclei before reaching cortex.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The thalamus is not a passive relay. Its nuclei gate information according to state, salience and cortical feedback, contributing to attention, arousal, memory and the coordination of distributed cognitive networks.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Each thalamus borders the third ventricle and is divided by internal medullary laminae into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups. Ventral posterior nuclei relay somatosensation; geniculate bodies relay visual and auditory information; ventral anterior and lateral nuclei participate in basal ganglia and cerebellar motor loops; anterior and mediodorsal nuclei support limbic and prefrontal functions; pulvinar and intralaminar nuclei contribute to association, attention and arousal. Clinical effects depend on laterality, vascular territory and network disconnection.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of a secure rail interchange: different platforms serve different destinations, while cortical feedback continually changes which trains are prioritised.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Thalamic injury can alter attention, memory, language, arousal, affect and sensory experience. Recognising a distributed thalamocortical pattern helps avoid mislabelling neurological changes as purely psychiatric.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A focal thalamic lesion may cause hemisensory loss, central pain, memory impairment, language or neglect-like symptoms, reduced alertness or executive change. Symptoms rarely identify a single nucleus without imaging and neurological examination.
sections.clinicalPearl: Bilateral paramedian thalamic injury can produce profound arousal and memory disturbance because it disrupts midline nuclei and their widespread cortical connections.
sections.clinicalExample: A person with a left paramedian thalamic infarct may present with fluctuating alertness, slowed initiation and memory difficulty despite relatively preserved primary strength.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas localisation supports hypothesis generation, not diagnosis. Thalamic nuclei are small, boundaries vary across atlases, and behavioural outcomes reflect connected cortical and subcortical systems.
sections.practicalExample: Use the thalamus atlas map to test whether a clinical pattern is anatomically coherent while considering network and medical alternatives.

anatomy.position: Paired ovoid structures on either side of the third ventricle, superior to the hypothalamus and medial to the internal capsule.

quiz.question: Which thalamic structure is the principal visual relay to primary visual cortex?
quiz.rationale: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays retinal information to primary visual cortex.

quiz.question: Why is the thalamus better described as a gate than a simple relay?
options: Corticothalamic and state-dependent signals modulate transmission
Every nucleus carries the same information
quiz.rationale: Thalamic transmission is dynamically shaped by cortical feedback, arousal and attention.

quiz.question: A unilateral posterolateral thalamic lesion most directly raises concern for which pattern?
quiz.rationale: Posterolateral thalamic sensory nuclei relay contralateral body and facial sensation.
